newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: INTERVIEW - Nampak upbeat on '98 profits.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Nampak upbeat on '98 profits.

text.p: South African packaging giant Nampak Ltd said on Wednesday it expects full year 1997 earnings to be uninspiring, but lower interest rates could be the key to a strong rebound in 1998.
Nampak's Managing Director Trevor Evans said 1997 had been tough for the group and the packaging industry as a whole due to stunted volume growth and low international packaging prices.
The situation had been worsened by a slow-down in the country's economy that was keeping consumers at bay.
"I expect Nampak's earnings next year to be considerably better than this year and the year after, assuming that the economy picks up," Evans told Reuters in an interview.
He said Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals's recent indications that interest rates could be cut before the end of the year boded well for an upturn in the industry.
But many market players are still concerned about how soon the effect of any cut will be felt by consumers.
"I think we really need to see something like a two or three percent cut and then I'll expect, a few months after that, benefit to start coming through," said Evans, adding:
"The debate is when will the benefit of lower interest rates start flowing through to the consumers' pockets."
Hopes of a cut in the country's interest rates mounted as signs emerge that the economy is quickly cooling off.
The general consensus on interest rates among economists is for a reduction in the third quarter, with a total of three cuts expected by June next year.
South Africa's Bank rate is currently at 17 percent, following a one percentage point hike last November.

Nampak, which has a share of about 43 percent of the South African packaging market, reported attributable earnings for the six months to March at 55.9 cents per share from 52.2 cents for the same period a year previously. The dividend was slightly up at 14.4 cents from 13.7 cents.

Nampak recently bought British firm Rexam Plc's remaining outstanding 50 percent stake in UK-based blow moulding firm Blowmocan, and it also has interests in major packaging companies in Botswana, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, Tanzania, Swaziland, Zambia and Zimbabwe.

But Evans said while Blowmocan, which makes dairy and juice containers, formed part of the group's strategic move into Europe, tough competition and the deregulation of the British milk industry continued to cloud its profitability.
Nampak and Rexam entered into the Blowmocan joint venture in February 1995.

"It's been making losses up to now, but we think it will break into a small profit next year," he said, adding Nampak had hoped, through the move, to plug into the blow-moulded beverage market as Britain shifted from glass and carton milk containers.
"One of our clients went into liquidation, while another problem is that one of the biggest players in the world, Tetrapak, came into that market," Evans said.
